title: Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde
author: Robert Louis Stevenson
openingText: Mr. Utterson the lawyer had a rugged face that no smile ever lit. He was cold, sparing and awkward in conversation, slow to show feeling, lean, tall, dusty and dreary, and yet somehow lovable. At friendly gatherings, when the wine was to his liking, something deeply human shone in his eye. It never found its way into his talk, but it spoke not only through these silent signs on his after-dinner face, but more often and more loudly in the actions of his life. He was strict with himself. He drank gin when he was alone, to punish his taste for fine vintages, and though he enjoyed the theatre, he had not set foot in one for twenty years. Toward others, however, he had a well-proven tolerance. He sometimes wondered, almost with envy, at the sheer force of spirits that went into their misdeeds, and in any extremity he was more inclined to help than to reprove. “I incline to Cain’s heresy,” he used to say, in his odd way. “I let my brother go to the devil in his own fashion.” Being such a man, he often found himself the last respectable acquaintance and the last good influence in the lives of people on the downward road. And to these, as long as they came to his chambers, he never showed the slightest change of manner.
about:
The lawyer Gabriel John Utterson investigates the connection between his old friend Dr. Henry Jekyll and the violent Edward Hyde. A strange will, an unsettling door, and conflicting accounts deepen his concern. After a murder, his search becomes urgent.

The story examines reputation, hidden desires, and responsibility. Jekyll hopes to indulge his evil side while protecting his respectable life. His experiment does not produce a wholly good Jekyll opposite an evil Hyde: Jekyll remains a mixture. His final account both acknowledges responsibility and tries to distance him from it.

angleCards.title: Respectability as repression.
angleCards.text: The central professional men place great value on reputation and discretion. Other characters include servants, women, and a child. Notice when protecting a good name becomes a reason to conceal troubling facts.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to read Jekyll and Hyde as a study of Victorian repression — the argument that a society obsessed with respectability creates the very monsters it fears.

angleCards.title: Hyde as freedom.
angleCards.text: Jekyll describes the first transformation as an experience of liberation — younger, lighter, more alive. Hyde is not simply evil; he is unrestrained. Track what Jekyll says about how it felt to be Hyde, before the horror set in.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to follow Jekyll's account of becoming Hyde — to understand what he found liberating about it and at what point liberation became imprisonment.

angleCards.title: The mystery structure.
angleCards.text: Stevenson tells the story as a detective plot: Utterson investigates, witnesses testify, documents are sealed and opened. The structure means the reader knows less than the characters for most of the book. Pay attention to what information is withheld and when it is released.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to read for the structure — how Stevenson controls information, delays the revelation, and uses the gap between what the reader knows and what the characters know to build dread.

angleCards.title: The body tells the truth.
angleCards.text: Hyde is physically repulsive to everyone who meets him, but no one can say exactly why. His appearance produces a visceral reaction of disgust that precedes any knowledge of his actions. What does it mean that evil has a body — that it can be felt before it is understood?
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to notice how the body functions in this story — how Hyde's physical presence communicates something that language cannot describe — and what Stevenson is saying about the relationship between morality and the physical.

cast.name: Gabriel Utterson
cast.description: A respectable London lawyer, old friend of Jekyll, and the story's primary viewpoint character. He is quiet, methodical, loyal, and deeply uneasy. The story follows his investigation into Jekyll's connection with Hyde, and his growing dread is the emotional register of the book. He represents the Victorian professional class at its most decent — and its most limited in the face of what it cannot explain.

cast.name: Dr. Henry Jekyll
cast.description: A successful physician and scientist, well-liked, generous, sociable — and concealing an inner life he considers incompatible with his public reputation. His experiment is not an accident but a deliberate attempt to separate the respectable and disreputable halves of his nature. He does not want to destroy Hyde; he wants to indulge Hyde without consequences. The discovery that this is impossible is the book's central horror.

cast.name: Edward Hyde
cast.description: The smaller, younger figure released by Jekyll's compound. Jekyll describes him as wholly evil, while Jekyll himself remains a mixture. Hyde tramples a child, murders Sir Danvers Carew, and becomes increasingly difficult for Jekyll to control.

cast.name: Dr. Hastie Lanyon
cast.description: A physician and former close friend of Jekyll who broke with him over what he considered Jekyll's unscientific speculations. When he finally witnesses the truth — a transformation he cannot deny and cannot explain — the shock kills him. His death is the book's most pointed argument: that there are things the rational, professional Victorian mind is not equipped to survive.

cast.name: Mr. Enfield
cast.description: Utterson's distant relative and Sunday walking companion. He has seen Hyde trample a child at a street corner, then enter a mysterious door to obtain money. His account sets Utterson's investigation in motion.

whyItMatters.title: The Language of Self-Deception
whyItMatters.body: Jekyll's confession shows a man who recognizes his guilt while trying to assign it to another self. His explanations invite a critical reading of how people describe their own choices.

whyItMatters.title: Horror in Familiar Surroundings
whyItMatters.body: Houses, offices, dinners, and friendships provide the setting for the horror. Familiar routines make small signs of change especially unsettling.

whyItMatters.title: Several Witnesses, Partial Knowledge
whyItMatters.body: The early witnesses cannot explain everything they see. The final documents give earlier details new significance and turn the mystery into an examination of responsibility.
